utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. All the accused are here. All the Defence teams are here in full. Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey. I understand - this is the reason we are starting a bit late, we usually don't do that - I understand there is a logistic problem in the sense that the witness is stuck in traffic. In the meantime we thought of starting just the same, and maybe see if there are any preliminaries you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, that's the information I have. We had the -- the witness after this was scheduled to be picked up at 9.30 -- excuse me, 9.15, so that witness should be coming in any second. It would get us out of order, but -- well, I think Madam Registrar has the latest on that. So we could -- we could go out of order and get started right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But still on the logistic level, what about the return travel arrangements for the witness that we are waiting for? Would that disrupt the travel arrangements, postponing his testimony to later, possibly not finishing with it today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My understanding is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I just want to make sure that that's okay with everybody. Would the suggestion that Mr. McCloskey is making go down well with the Defence teams? Are there any objections from any one of you? I hear none. So we can proceed along those lines. Mr. McCloskey, yesterday you filed a Prosecution motion requesting protective measures for Witness 157 with an ex parte annex. When do you propose to produce this -- this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, let's go into private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness, the second witness is here, but he was taken by surprise, being told that he is going to testify immediately, and so he is being spoken to by the Victims and Witnesses to make him feel somewhat relaxed. But he is here and we can start with his testimony soon. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Further problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, nothing significant. Apparently the witness beat the interpreter here, and so -- and is a bit nervous and would like to know what's going on. So we're just waiting for the interpreter so we can tell him. But it should just be a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst we are waiting, it's the registrar's intention through Your Honour that Mr. Krgovic needs some technical assistance, please, with his computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Usher, or Madam Registrar. Thank you. Do you have any problems, I'm referring to the accused, with your -- with your computer set-up? Seems Mr. Krgovic only. The United Kingdom and the United States are divided by the same language, but the way we -- we have it, page 3, line 21, I don't want any misunderstandings. I mean no one should take it as meaning that some violence has taken place, basically means that he has arrived before the interpreter has. But for the record, I want to make sure that we haven't had any unfortunate -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we are in fine shape. Mr. Vanderpuye didn't look too good, but I think everyone's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose someone from the Victims and Witnesses Unit speaks his language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's who we were counting on. Apparently they dropped him and -- and he was by himself when found by Mr. Vanderpuye. And that's very unusual. I know they must be running around like crazy this morning. So...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. All right. And again, being dropped is to be taken metaphorically and not literally. Figuratively speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm slipping backwards in my diction, but hopefully by 9.30 I won't be saying anything anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we check again, please. Again I apologise to. Again, I apologise to everyone for this. We are trying to do our best. For the record, Mr. Vanderpuye has entered the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is Witness number 156. I just want a confirmation that this is Witness 156, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He is, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So he's got a pseudonym and face -- facial distortion only; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... earlier than you expected. I welcome you to this Tribunal. This is the Popovic et al case, and you are one of the Prosecution witnesses. I apologise to you for bringing you earlier than expected and starting your evidence earlier than expected, but we had a problem this morning with the previous witness, so in order not to waste time or lose time, we decided that since you were coming here in any case, we start with your testimony. I am sure that I have your full understanding. Okay. Thank you. So good morning to you. You are about to start giving evidence. Mr. Vanderpuye will be examining you in chief. Before you do so, however, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. This is being handed to you. Please stand up, read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us that will be speaking the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. We have made some arrangements to protect your identity, that is your name will not be used, we will use a pseudonym, and also your face will be distorted, we have facial distortion. In other words, I think this has been explained to you. I just want to make sure that this arrangement is to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, he is all yours. How long do you expect your direct to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I expect it will last about an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Usher, may I have the pseudonym sheet, please, shown to the witness. It's P02434 for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, before you proceed, Mr. McCloskey, I think that -- or rather the registrar, I don't think I put the responsibility on you. Madam Registrar, I think we will require an explanation from whoever is responsible for the transportation of the witness as to what happened. We just want to make sure that what happened was justified and not the result of some negligence. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I -- I have those answers and I can give them to you at appropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not right now. Okay. Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Madam Usher, could I, please, have PO2434 shown to the witness. Sir, could you, please, have a look at that piece of paper and can you confirm without reading what's on it, that you are the person that's named in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Have that shown to counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Again I apologise to you, Mr. Vanderpuye, for butting in like this. I mean it's not my style but there are moments when it is needed. Witness, testifying in these proceedings and in any proceedings is not easy for any witness. So if at any time you need a short break or a long break or you are feeling tired or you are not feeling too well, please do tell us and we will accommodate you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Witness. I would just ask you to try to keep your voice up, if you can, to move a little closer to the microphone so that everyone can hear you. The interpreters are trying to interpret simultaneously, so if you would allow just a short pause between the question and answer, so that we have time to catch up. Also, I wanted to point out to you that because of the measures we've taken to protect your identity, if you feel that the question that I ask you or any counsel asks you calls for a response that may reveal aspects of your identity, such as where you live or people that you know or places that you've been, just let us know and I will ask the Trial Chamber if they would consider moving into private session so that we can discuss those matters more freely. I'm just going to ask you a couple of questions and then I will ask the Trial Chamber, with the Trial Chamber's indulgence, to move into private session. First, are you a -- are you a Bosnian by nationality, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: I'm not in the best of health, I'm coughing a lot, but I'm better than I was three days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you feel able to testify in these proceedings at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So let me ask you, are you a Bosnian by nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May we move into private session, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I would like to direct your attention, if I could, to the events of July 11th, 1995. In relation to the events concerning Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: That day, the 11th of July, 1995, I gathered hay and prepared food for cattle on that day. And then I went into the house, took a back-pack, and set out. We were told that there would be a gathering at Jaglici, and I went to Jaglici with my wife and two daughters. We came to a point where we had to separate. The elderly, civilian, and women were going to Potocari, and we were going to the woods. However, I was going to go to Potocari as well, but my back-pack was with my neighbour on a horse, and it -- it went in the direction of the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just slow you down for a second. And maybe we can take this a little bit step-by-step. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated that you were told that there would be a gathering at Jaglici at some point on that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall how you received that information, who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: I was busy with the hay, and then my daughter came and said that a neighbour of ours was killed and she said an order was issued to go, because Srebrenica had fallen. I went into the house, I packed some food and clothing, and then we set out. When we were near Ravne Njive, women, children, and the elderly were to go to Potocari, to the UNPROFOR base. I went with the army because my back-pack was on a horse and the bread was there, so I didn't go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you learned from your daughter that Srebrenica had fallen, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: Yes. I guess somebody in the village came in and told them that, but I wasn't in the village, I was out in the field on my property.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, after your daughter told you that, it seems that you decided that you would leave. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, in deciding whether or not to leave, did you leave immediately or did you -- did you leave a little bit later after your daughter told you what had happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: I just gathered some food and I went to the barn to release the cattle. I came across my brother-in-law who said, "Don't do anything with the cattle." The cattle remained in the barn. And then we set out. It could have been around 7.00 or 7.30 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you see any other people leaving the area in which you were around that time or throughout that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: They set out before me, before I moved. There were columns, both in front of me and behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you at any time consider the possibility of actually staying in the area in which you were at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: Well, I thought that we would remain, because it was a protected enclave. Women, children, and the elderly went to a location that was safe. In my village, nine neighbours went to Potocari to the UNPROFOR base to the protected enclave, and none of the nine are alive today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, at the time that your daughter told you that Srebrenica had fallen, I assume that you understood that to mean that it had fallen to the Serb forces. Is that a fair thing to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: Well, naturally. Had it not been fallen to Serb forces, we wouldn't have gone away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you leave that area on that day because you were ordered to leave that area, or for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: Because Srebrenica was a protected enclave, and then they said that the Serb forces entered Srebrenica and as soon as the town fell, the villages fell as well. So we agreed to withdraw from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that women and children and the elderly went to Potocari. Now, among your -- among your family, did any of your family go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: My brother and his son, and then two neighbours. None of them are alive nowadays. This is just from my family; brother, cousin, and another two relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you indicated that those people went to Potocari because it was safe. Did you know at that time that it would be safe for them to go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: Naturally it was safe, because UNPROFOR was there, and it was a protected enclave. So they were hoping that it would be safer for them there. And you can see just how safe it was for them. They're all gone now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, at some point you indicated that after you left you -- you separated from some of the people that you were with. Could you tell us a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: There were a lot of us in columns moving towards Jaglici and Potocari. I split from my family near the village called Ravne Njive. I went to Jaglici and they went to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you go to Jaglici alone or -- well, I know you went with a column, you indicated that, but did you go with anybody that you knew? And please don't tell us what their names are.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: Well, in the column that I was, almost everybody around me were my neighbours. They were all familiar faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Tell us what happened -- tell us what happened on your way to Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: On the way to Jaglici we had a safe passage. There was no hinderance. We arrived at Jaglici and it was night-time. We spent the entire night in Jaglici. On the 12th I went from Jaglici at around 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: You mean from Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, from Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: We left Jaglici and it was 20 to 1.00. I asked a forester what time it was, and he told me it was 20 to 1.00. And we set out towards Buljim. I didn't know what Buljim was, and this is where there was the first ambush. People were killed there. I went with some of my neighbours towards the river. I didn't know the area. I didn't know where I was going. We went down the river and on both banks there were dead bodies. We came to a forest. We didn't know where we were going. And then we came across a neighbour of mine whose wife is from Kamenica, and I asked him, "Where are we?" And he said, "We are near Kamenica." And this is where we were when the night fell. At night they started shooting near a hill. We started moving towards the sound of shooting. We didn't know who was shooting. We could hear a Praga firing and then we went back. This group of ours, there were perhaps six to seven of us in our group. There was a lot of shooting, bullets whizzing by my head, and I took shelter, I lay down. I thought that that was the safest thing to do. And I thought that everybody else had done the same. When I got up, I didn't know what time of night it was, I called out the names of my friends and none of them responded. I got up and I could hear occasional bursts of fire and I started moving in that direction, and then all of a sudden I heard, "Don't shoot. This is our people." And then I said, "Who is it?" And then they said, "Come up here." And then I said, "Who is talking to me?" And the man gave his name and then I approached him and I sat next to him. And he asked me whether I had anything in my back-pack. I said I had some meat, I had some bread. He said, "I'm hungry." I said, "Well, here, have some." Then he started eating and then we went from there. There were so many dead bodies that you could step from one to the other one. Then we moved some 500 metres and then people were saying, "Brothers, help us." And you know people were killed. It was night-time. There were a lot of wounded people. And then I separated from this man who called me. I spent the whole night wandering through the wounded looking for some familiar faces, but I didn't find anybody familiar. Then they said that we should carry the wounded to a hill above Kamenica. And then it dawned. We came to that hill. I didn't know where I was. That was an unfamiliar terrain for me. And I saw that people were lining up there. I recognised a man from a neighbouring village, and then I came across three neighbours of mine down there. I asked them, "Where are you going?" They said, "To line up." Then the four of us went back and they said, "There are a lot of people from our village there." So we went there and we found a large group of people. You couldn't count them all, there were so many of them. I found a man who used to work as a male nurse in our town, and then a person who was a teacher, then I found an Imam who worked as an Imam in Vlasenica municipality. And then I also found a policeman from my village. So we were there. The nurse, the male nurse dressed the wounds of the wounded. They carried -- they brought the wounded to him and he took care of them. We sat there. I didn't know what time of the day it was, and then all of a sudden from the hill above us, there was an oak forest and we heard bursts of fire and they started saying, "Surrender, surrender." We started going down to the meadow, to the asphalt road. And all we could hear were the calls to surrender. They surrounded us there. Some people starting raising up towels and T-shirts and saying don't shoot, we will surrender. There were a lot of wounded there when they surrendered us, and they ordered us to carry the wounded. Then the forester, the one who told me that it was 20 to 1.00, I saw him again and he had a blanket and he was carrying Mujo, his brother, who was wounded. And he said, "Please don't leave my brother. We were ordered to carry the wounded." I knew that man, the man who was wounded, and we went down to the river, to some river. We were bringing the wounded down to the river and then we were crossing it and then there were two Serb soldiers and we went by them. They searched our pockets, just to make sure we didn't have a knife, a pistol, a hand-grenade. They searched through our back-packs or whatever belongings we had. They asked for money from us. I had 100 German marks in my pocket, and then I also had 600 German marks, or rather, 400 franks plus 200 German marks and it was sewn into the lining and I gave him some money and then I said, "I don't have anymore." We crossed the asphalt road with our arms raised up. We came to a meadow. I don't know what that meadow was called. I didn't know where we were until I escaped from the warehouse. And after I escaped from the warehouse, I learned that we had been at Lolici. This is what the man who was with me told me. I didn't know Lolici. We went across the asphalt road, we sat on the meadow. And there was a huge crowd of people there. I couldn't count them. Didn't even occur to me to count them. I listened to the people talking around me, the nurse and the teacher and a policeman. They were whispering among themselves, saying, "There must be 2.000 people here." I didn't count because it didn't even occur to me. How they came to that figure, I have no idea whether there was more or less, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you for a moment, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I didn't want to interrupt the witness's answer, but it seems to me that we are going into very, very great detail now about the column, a subject about which the Prosecution have made a number of stipulations in this case, and about which you have voiced the concern that it is not the proper subject of cross-examination. Now, either this is relevant to the indictment or it isn't. And if it isn't, I don't really see what is the purpose of extensive examination-in-chief about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Since I know that's related to the last witness, we are through that area now. We are at the meadow, and we -- and I know Mr. Vanderpuye is -- and the witness will try to stay to the areas that are important, though -- and -- and we're doing our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In the same context, I, having listened to what you said, Mr. Haynes, I do want to dispel from your minds any idea that the existence of a column or the way they proceeded or its composition are irrelevant to -- to the case. I mean they are highly relevant, but what I said yesterday still stands. I mean what has been stipulated and what has already to an extent been decided upon by the Trial Chamber in its decision on adjudicated facts ought to be respected, and unnecessary -- unnecessary examination and cross-examination should be avoided. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. Please go straight now to...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't aware of the previous discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were not here yesterday, obviously, so I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to focus your attention, if I could, at the period of time from your surrender up until the time that you were at the meadow. I just want to backtrack a little bit. Now, you said that when you surrendered, was it that you were escorted an asphalt road or is that the place where you actually surrendered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: We surrendered up there in the meadow, and they followed the column, descending down to the river and carrying the wounded. They told us to carry the wounded. As we descended to the river, we had left the wounded across the river. We crossed the river and then the two of them searched us and took our money. We tied our hands above our necks. We crossed the asphalt road and then we sat in the meadow. They brought people there in groups and individually. Later on I saw that they brought two neighbours of mine, and then there was a large group of people that gathered in that meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: And they were around us, their soldiers. I can't say that they beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just hang on a second. Did you see what happened to the wounded people at the time that you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: When we sat in the meadow, they took the wounded to a house to the right of us. What happened in the house I don't know, because we sat in the meadow. There was a tank on the right and one on the left. They twice brought in a water truck, which sprayed us, because it was very hot. The tank that was on the right pointed its barrel at us twice. There was a man there in civilian uniform, and he said, "You stupid men, just raise that barrel up." It didn't shoot at us. This was just meant to abuse us. And then the soldiers who were around us provided cigarettes to those who smoked. They didn't beat us. There was a man in front of me in the third row. I didn't know him. The children brought water. He asked for water. And then a Serb soldier kicked him in the head, and then another one hit him on the side of the head. He started bleeding and then one grabbed him by the tie, the other one grabbed him by his legs, and they moved him some six to seven metres away and shot a burst of fire into him. We left the meadow and his body remained lying there. We sat there in the meadow and then they recognised the policeman. A Serb soldier called him by his name and he approached them. He said hello to them. And then the two of them greeted him. They hugged him, they kissed him, and I felt good about it because I thought that here these people are friends, and they will release us. And then they took him to a house on the left. He stayed there for about an hour, hour and a half, and then he came back with three soldiers. And he stood by the tank and called his brother. He said, "Give me my jacket." The brother came across and brought him the jacket. They asked who this man is. And he said, "My brother." Then he turned around and called out the third brother. Then they asked again who is he? And he said brother too. And they said, "Well, all of you can go." And the three of them were taken above the house where the wounded were, the three soldiers and the three of them, and they have not been heard from ever since. I didn't hear any shoots, but to this day, nobody has ever heard of them. We continuing sitting in that meadow and then General Mladic arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just stop you right there for a minute. With respect to the soldiers, can you just describe to the Court, first of all, were they in uniform, and if you can remember what the uniforms looked like, could you just describe that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: All of them were in multi-coloured uniforms. They were young, had regular crew-cuts, and were properly shaved. It was the regular army. When Mladic came, he stood in front of us and addressed us. The first thing he said is, "Do you know me?" Some people said yes, we do, some people kept quiet. I didn't know anything. I just kept quiet. All I thought was my fate. His first words were, "Naser has deserted you. He fled to Tuzla. It's not a good idea to fight with Serbia [as interpreted]. We have almost evacuated your families. They are accommodated in Tuzla, Kladanj, and another place. Most likely, within a day or two, you will follow and all of you will be able to find your families. Nobody will beat you, nobody will provoke you. We will provide food to you. It's very hot here where you are. We will find cooler accommodation for you." Then an applause ensued and people said, "Thank you, comrade general." I raised my arm. He said, "What?" I said -- I raised my foot and I said, "Comrade general, you can see that I'm bare footed. I have shoes in my back-pack and I would like to put them on." And he said, "You will get your shoes." I said, "Thank you, comrade general." Then he left. Then after some 15 to 20 minutes, the man who was in civilian uniform said that we were to be searched, and I heard them address one person as Madzarevic. I didn't know him. One of them was blond, had his hair tied in a ponytail with a black ribbon. They searched us and they found money in my lining. They find 600 German marks, my daughter's necklace and 10 gold coins. They confiscated that from me. After they searched us, the same men in civilian uniform had a German shepherd. He also had a machine-gun, and he was some 60 to 70 metres away. I didn't know whether it was machine-gun 53 or 74 -- or rather 84. Then he said that we should line up in columns by four. A column started forming and I was maybe somewhere in the middle of the column. On both sides of the column there was a soldier --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there if I could again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't want to interrupt the witness, particularly not my colleague, but I have one small intervention on the transcript. It is on page 21, line 4. The witness said -- well, quoting Mladic, he said, "It is not a good idea to fight with Serbs." And here it says "with Serbia." That's the only thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't confirm that obviously because I don't understand the language. But, Witness, when you were telling us repeating the words that according to you General Mladic pronounced at the time, did he say it's not a good idea to fight with Serbia or it is not a good idea to fight with Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he came and addressed us, the first thing he said, but let me repeat it again, "Naser has deserted you. He fled to Tuzla. It's not a good idea to fight with a Serb." With a Serb, not a good idea. Later on I realised what it is that he said because they let us go in a triangle and they cut the road. So he was right, because what he said was that the cattle cannot leave the corral until an opening is created. And the same applied to us. We could not get out of that circle until they made an opening for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have a break now, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's -- how much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least 10, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So instead of having the usual break at 10.30, we will have it now. And it will be a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Are you better, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right. I mean it's not the best that it could be, but it's all right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure he will -- when you give your answers, try to move near the microphones as much as you can. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we go into private session for just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I think before the break you had just started to talk about being part of a column at the meadow and being lined up in groups of four or four abreast. Could you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: From the meadow, there was an order to get into a column, four abreast. The column formed. I was perhaps somewhere after the first half of the column, and we were moving towards Kravica, but I didn't know that. It was the first time that I had come to Kravica. When we were approaching Kravica, there was an UNPROFOR APC on the right-hand side. Some soldiers were standing around there. Nobody reacted in any way. We were passing by. We came in front of the warehouse. There was a bus parked in front of the warehouse, and we were passing between the bus and the warehouse. I passed the first entrance, and I came to the second entrance. And that's where I went in, through the second entrance door. And it was all full up to the second entrance. And a person called me who had been with us. He said, "Come and sit next to me." I said, "I want to lean against the wall because my back hurts." So I carried on along the warehouse. A soldier who was standing at the entrance, he cursed God or something at me and he said, "Sit down." And I said, "I want to lean against the wall because my back hurts." And I came to a corner and I sat and leaned against the wall. When the warehouse was filled, when the last person came in, he had nowhere to sit. And that soldier kicked him in the lower back. He cursed the son and said, "Sit down." He said, "Well, you can see I don't have anywhere to sit." And he fired a burst of fire and that knocked him down and then there was a burst of fire, all kinds of weapons. I just bent my head in the corner. I closed my eyes. The shooting went on almost until night. They would stop a little bit and you couldn't see anything in the -- in the warehouse because it was very dusty. I saw this last man who had come in. When the night fell, the shooting quieted down. You could hear them in front of the warehouse, laughing, talking. I was lying in the warehouse. There was blood all underneath me. My whole right-hand side was soaked in blood. I brought that shirt and sweater to Zepa and they could see what my shirt and sweater were like. I was lying there during the whole night. I was brought there on the 13th to the warehouse. On the 14th, the whole day, I spent in the warehouse, amongst the dead. And then when the 14th was over, at night, I had this kind of image as if they were drinking water, and I got up and moved through the dead. I found a neighbour of mine. He said, "Where are you going?" I said, "I want to drink water." He said, "Forget the water. Just lie down." So I lay down, and he lay down next to me. I asked him, "Are you wounded?" He said, "No." He asked me if I was and I said, "No." It was already dawn. You could sense it through the windows at the door that it was dawn. He got up. I said, "Where are you going?" He said, "I want to urinate --" I apologise "-- so that I could drink." I said, "Lie down." But he was cut down by a burst of fire and he fell. I took him by the knee. After about 10 or 15 minutes his body was stiff, not moving. I pulled two dead bodies over me and I spent the entire day there. In the morning, when it got light, you could see that it got light, they asked are there any unhurt people there? They can come out and they can join their army. People came out. I don't know who went out and how many of them. I didn't see and I didn't look. A truck engine started and I don't know which direction it went in. I don't know what was happening outside, just what I was able to hear. I don't know what time of the day it was. They said, "Are there any wounded? They can come out and we can take them to the hospital." The wounded came out. I don't know of those how many of them came out. They were killed. And then you couldn't hear anyone in the warehouse, not even a moan or a shout. One of them started to shout out, "Salko, Salko, Salko." He shouted it 10 or 15 times. They cursed his Turkish mother. And he was cut down by shots. You couldn't hear anyone moaning or shouting. Maybe an hour or an hour and a half passed. One of them started to call out "Adila, water. Adila, water." He was so exhausted that they could hardly understand it. They cursed his Islam tribe and he was cut down by a burst of fire. You couldn't hear anybody any more than you could hear some kind of noise or something. I didn't move. I didn't look. And then when it was dark again, I could hear a command, "Park the loader. Wash the asphalt. Cover the dead with hay." They threw hay all over us and then I thought, Why didn't I get killed? I thought that they were going to set it on fire and that I would be burned alive. But they didn't set the hay on fire. When it was night, you couldn't hear anyone in front of the warehouse. You couldn't hear any talk or any machinery. You could just hear an occasional vehicle pass by on the asphalt. But it wasn't very frequent. Maybe it was 12.30, after midnight, and I started to move. I pulled out from among the dead bodies because I couldn't stand it anymore in the blood. And I was stiff. I got up and I moved around a little bit, and I sat down. Had someone taken me by the hand and said, Let's go, I wouldn't have been able to go. I was so stiff. I sat for an hour or two and I was rubbing my legs and my arms and I came to a little bit, and I was able to go. But I didn't know where to go. It was as if somebody had thrown me out of an airplane. I was sitting and thinking what I could do. And I could hear some whispering and I moved towards this whispering and I thought when they had killed everyone they could kill me too. But I found two people sitting up inside, one of them was young, tall. Another one -- the other one was my age, maybe. And I said, "Let's run." And this young, tall man said, "We can't go together. Where are you from?" He said, "I'm from Lolici." I said, "Well, let me go with you. You know the area around here." And he said, "Well, we can't go together." I said, "I don't know where I can go." I tell you we can't go together. Then I asked the other one, "Where are you from?" He just made this gesture with his shoulders. He said, "That's Muskic Ramiz from Cerska. He can't hear very well." Again I asked him if I could go with him. "I tell you, we can't go together. Go across the asphalt, you will find a path to the river, and then in 15 or 20 minutes, I will follow you." And I decided to go. I decided. I got up because he didn't let me go with him. I left through the same door that I came in. There was a loader parked there. It was dark. I passed the loader and I stepped out with my right leg first on the asphalt. I remember that. I didn't see anyone on the right-hand side of the asphalt until somebody shouted stop. I didn't see them before that. He shouted, "Stop" and I lay down. The second time he shouted, "Get up, get up." I kept lying down. The third time he said, sharply, "Get up." I jumped up. The other one just lay down next to me, behind the warehouse, the warehouse I left behind on my left-hand side. I came down into a river. I just put my head in the water to drink because my mouth was totally dry from the dust. I couldn't speak. The other guy next to me went into the river. We crossed the river. We went into this corn. We left the corn. There was a road between the corn and the woods. I took him by the hand. He couldn't hear me. "Where are we going?" He said, "Kaldrmica, Cerska, Baljkovica." Just keep to the left, keep to the left. I couldn't communicate with him. He couldn't hear me, and I couldn't speak loudly. We took the road. There was a bend in the road around the cornfield. Again I went down, I drank water. I went back. We sat under a tree, and we could hear bursts of fire from the warehouse. But one burst of fire, another burst of fire, and nobody came after us. When we left there were no bullets behind us. Nobody was heard to say "Stop." I can't say, perhaps somebody was humane. They could have killed us with a stone, never mind with a rifle, but nobody fired a shot behind us, after us, and nobody shouted for us to stop. It began to rain. We went to a tree that had been knocked over. We were wet. A few days we were walking around in that area. Let's go back. He just kept saying, "Baljkovica, Kaldrmica, Cerska." He just kept saying, "I know that. We couldn't cross the asphalt." He brought me to some place where I found a couple of neighbours from my village and they told me there was a forester in Srebrenica. He had a transistor radio, a pocket one, and he said Zepa hasn't fallen yet. Well, I wanted to get to this forester because he knew the terrain, just so he could take me out of Pobudje. The forester didn't come there and at night about 30 people collected there in that area where there were some walls and there were frying some mushrooms and stuff. Then in the morning I found three people from the Bratunac municipality. I called them, Let's go. And then this man said, from my neighbouring village, "My child can't leave hungry." He had a small son with him, about 15 years old. He was worn down by hunger. But he's going to die here of hunger. There is nothing here, there is no corn, there is no wheat, there is no potatoes. Let's go. He said, "My boy can't go hungry." And then with these two from the Bratunac municipality, I decided to go. Do you know the road? I don't. Two deaf and dumb men, both of them from Cerska, came and they knew this man who came out with me. The three of them were together and they kept saying, "Kaldrmica, Cerska, Baljkovica." I said good-bye to them, and I went with these two people from the Bratunac municipality. I didn't know the road. They don't know the road. You could hear bursts of fire above this village of Jelah. We hid in some nettles in a garden and you could hear music. And then we went up through an oak forest. We met a young man. He said, "Where are you going?" I said, "We're going to Srebrenica. Where are you from? From Jagodnja." I couldn't believe him. He said, "Do you know Hasim, the forester?" He said, "It is my first neighbour." I said, "It is my neighbour too. I don't know who was leading me. Who would I be going with? How many children does Hasim have? Tell them the names." And he told the names, what's his wife's name, and he told me the wife's name, Munevera called Banana. And me and these two people and him, now there were four of us joined together. We came up to that hill above Jelah and then I saw eight dead bodies there and this man, this young man from Jagodnja escaped from there. I said, "Do you know where Rahunici is? Over there. That's where the mosque was."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I just stop you for a moment. If I could, I would like to -- if I may, and I don't -- I know you have a lot to say, and it's all very important. But I'd like to show you some photographs, if I could, of the warehouse. Just so that you can tell the Court and give the Court an idea of where you were when the incident transpired there. I think the first thing I'd like to show you is 65 ter 15 -- 1565. If I could just have that on the monitor, please. All right. Can you see the photograph on your monitor, sir? I would like to have the witness also mark the photograph, if I could. I think he may require some assistance. All right. Are you all right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: I'm all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. First, do you recognise what's depicted in this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And just tell the Court what it is, so that it's clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: I came from this direction. I passed this entrance --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just tell us what it is that you see on there. Well, let me ask you this: Is that where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: According to me, yes. But the -- this door does not seem to me to be the door. The door seems to be different than when we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you to mark this photograph in a way. Do you recognise on this photograph the door that you entered or left from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: On this photograph, that's where the bus was parked, and I passed this entrance door and I got in to -- through this entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to ask if you could mark --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that what I'm seeing? Is there a mark on there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There no marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is a tiny mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you put -- let's see, the letters -- I don't know, "I-n", that would be a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make it one letter. Make it "E", entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Only because --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. E for entry. Could you write that letter, please, at the door that you have entered from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: Here, should I put it? [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you make an arrow pointing to that door, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: That's the door that I went out through.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: I went this way and I came to this door and I entered through this door. There was a soldier here, and another one here. I passed between them and I went to the extreme -- to the corner at the far end of the warehouse, close to the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's see if we can take this one step at a time. Okay? So first, we'll talk about the door. If you could mark -- it seems to me that you have marked the door that you entered, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: I passed this one. This is the first door. And then I came in through the second door. And I also came out through that same door.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So what I would like you to mark then, if we can -- if we could do that, is "I/O" right on that door. If he could, yeah.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we -- I think we may need a different photograph to do this, but could you mark this PW-156 A in the top left-hand corner? That seems to be the cleanest place to mark it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: P, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir. That's just fine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: P. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah, that's fine. All right. Can we -- is it possible to have another frame of the same photograph because I would like him to make additional markings, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He needs to put 156.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, he does. Okay.

utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Thank you, Mr. President. I think we can file this one away and proceed with a -- I guess another version of this same photograph for him to mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, if you are able, could you mark on the photograph where it is you saw the loader, and you could probably just designate that with the letter L.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: It was night. I remember well. And the loader was then on this side. I came out through this door and the loader was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you mark that with the letter L, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you also put the letter B where it is you saw the bus, if you can, on this -- on this frame.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: The bus perhaps was here. We were passing by there, and the bus maybe was there. We just passed between, between the warehouse and the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you put the letter B at that location, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And could you also write in the top-left corner "PW-156"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-156

utterances.text: Okay. Could you just mark on the top of this photograph on the left, "PW-156," please.
